reader.title: Attempted lynching of Banks in Texas
bases: A mob gathered at Banks's house resolved to kill him, and after he surrendered a mob threatened to take him from jail and hang him; he survived and was driven from the state (A2).

A mob twice set out to kill Banks, first at his house and then by threatening to take him from jail and hang him, and claimed a search warrant for stolen beef and hides as its justification, but Banks survived (A2); this is an attempted lynching, not a completed one.

The case is known only from one passage in a New York Tribune interview (A2), apparently told by a Texas Republican who had fled the state (A1); no Texas, wire or Black-press report was found, and the reprints of the interview (A3, A4) leave the passage out.

summary.text: The attempted lynching of Banks was a mob attack on a Black farmer at his home in Texas, reported in August 1880, followed by a threat to hang him in jail.
Banks killed a man named Bates during the attack, was not indicted, and left the state on the sheriff's advice.
The New York Tribune printed the case as one example of political violence in Texas.
Banks was described as one of the most respected Black men in his county, who since emancipation had bought a small farm stocked with cattle and horses.
The account names no county or date.
Early one evening Banks overheard a mob gathering around his house, its members telling each other to be sure to kill him, "for we want him out of the road."
The start of the account is lost, but Banks killed "young Bates", escaped through the woods to the county seat, and surrendered to the sheriff.
For three days the killing kept the county in intense excitement, and a mob threatened to take Banks from the jail and hang him; fearing a lynching, the sheriff moved him to the jail at Houston.
Banks was held at Houston until the grand jury met, and it found no indictment against him.
Believing he would be killed on sight, the sheriff advised him to leave Texas, and Banks left his family and nearly ripe crops "without a cent in his pocket."
No arrest of any member of the mob is reported.
The only known report closes a New York Tribune interview of 23 August 1880 with Amos F. Bissell, a federal customs inspector who said he had fled Texas over a Republican speech.
The Tribune headed it "DEMOCRATIC VIOLENCE IN TEXAS," and the passage calls the Banks case one of "several other cases, similar to this, well known to have occurred in Texas."
No Texas paper, wire report or Black newspaper carrying the case was found.
The mob claimed a warrant to search Banks's house for stolen beef and cattle hides.
The Tribune account says the warrant, though dated before the affair, was obtained from a constable two days after it.

accounts.label: Bissell interview (New York Tribune)
accounts.gist: A mob gathered at the home of a respected Black farmer intending to kill him; he killed young Bates in self-defence, surrendered, was nearly lynched in jail, was not indicted, and was forced into exile.

accounts.label: Mob's claim
accounts.gist: The mob said it had a warrant to search Banks's house for stolen beef and cattle hides; the same account says the warrant was backdated, issued two days after the affair.

framing.detail: The Republican New York Tribune ran the case under 'DEMOCRATIC VIOLENCE IN TEXAS' and 'THE REBEL DASH FOR POWER', presenting Banks as respectable and the killing as self-defence.
